blocks.text: Once a month, in a woman of reproductive age, a single egg is released from a pea-sized follicle and, two weeks later, the lining of the uterus is shed unless a pregnancy has begun. These two events, hundreds of kilometres apart in cellular terms, are choreographed by a handful of hormones that switch from braking the pituitary to pressing its accelerator at exactly the right moment.

blocks.markdown: **Two cycles, one rhythm.** The **ovarian cycle** describes events in the ovary: follicle growth, ovulation and the corpus luteum. The **menstrual (uterine) cycle** describes the resulting changes in the endometrium. A typical cycle lasts about **28 days** (the normal range is wide, roughly 21-35 days), counted from the first day of menstrual bleeding (**day 1**). Three phases are defined: the **follicular phase**, **ovulation**, and the **luteal phase**. The **luteal phase** is fairly constant at about **14 days**, so differences in cycle length come mainly from the follicular phase.

blocks.title: Two-cell, two-gonadotrophin model
blocks.text: Oestradiol is made by cooperation of two follicular cell types. Theca cells, stimulated by LH, convert cholesterol to androgens. Granulosa cells, stimulated by FSH, express aromatase and convert those androgens to oestradiol. LH therefore drives the supply of substrate and FSH drives its conversion.

blocks.markdown: **Follicular phase (about days 1-14).** At the end of the previous cycle, falling oestradiol, progesterone and inhibin A release the pituitary from inhibition, so **FSH rises** and recruits a cohort of follicles. As follicles grow, granulosa cells make **oestradiol** and **inhibin B**, which inhibit FSH by negative feedback. This lowers FSH, so only the follicle most sensitive to FSH, the **dominant follicle**, continues to grow while the others become atretic. Rising oestradiol from the dominant follicle produces the next steps: it makes the **endometrium proliferate**, and later it triggers the LH surge.

**Ovulation and the LH surge.** Normally oestradiol inhibits the pituitary (negative feedback). However, when oestradiol rises to a high level and stays high for about 2 days (as the dominant follicle matures), the effect on the pituitary and hypothalamus **switches to positive feedback**: GnRH pulses and, importantly, gonadotroph sensitivity to GnRH increase, causing a large **LH surge** with a smaller FSH surge. The surge completes the first meiotic division of the oocyte, activates enzymes that digest the follicle wall and, about **36 hours after the onset of the surge**, causes **ovulation** (release of a secondary oocyte arrested in metaphase of meiosis II). It also triggers **luteinisation**: the remaining granulosa and theca cells become the **corpus luteum**.

**Luteal phase (about days 15-28).** The corpus luteum secretes large amounts of **progesterone** and also oestradiol and inhibin A, which together inhibit LH and FSH by negative feedback and so prevent new follicle development. Progesterone raises basal body temperature by about 0.3-0.5 degrees Celsius. If fertilisation and implantation do not occur, the corpus luteum degenerates (luteolysis) after about 14 days; progesterone and oestradiol fall, and the cycle restarts with a rise in FSH. If pregnancy occurs, human chorionic gonadotrophin from the embryo maintains the corpus luteum.

blocks.caption: Ovarian and endometrial events across the cycle (28-day cycle).
rows: Functional layer shed; basal layer retained
Proliferation of glands, stroma and spiral arteries; thickening
Rupture of follicle, release of oocyte
Tortuous glands secreting glycogen-rich fluid, oedematous stroma, coiled spiral arteries

blocks.markdown: **Endometrial structure and ovarian hormones.** The endometrium has a **functional layer** (superficial, sheds each cycle) and a **basal layer** (deep, regenerates the functional layer). **Oestradiol** drives the **proliferative phase**: epithelial and stromal proliferation, growth of straight glands and spiral arteries, and increases progesterone receptor expression. **Progesterone** drives the **secretory phase**: glands become tortuous and secrete glycogen-rich fluid, the stroma becomes oedematous and the spiral arteries coil, creating a state ready for implantation. When the corpus luteum fails and progesterone and oestradiol fall, spiral arteries constrict, the functional layer becomes ischaemic and is shed as **menstruation** (about 3-7 days).

blocks.caption: Because the luteal phase is nearly constant (about 14 days), ovulation occurs about 14 days before the next menstruation.

blocks.title: Timing ovulation in a 30-day cycle
blocks.prompt: A woman has regular 30-day cycles. On which day of the cycle is ovulation expected, and how long is her follicular phase?

steps.text: Ovulation is expected around day 16, since the luteal phase is about 14 days.
Follicular phase length is the time from day 1 to ovulation, about 16 days, which is longer than in a 28-day cycle (14 days); this shows variation in cycle length comes from the follicular phase.

blocks.answer: Ovulation is expected around day 16, with a follicular phase of about 16 days.

blocks.title: Predicting the consequence of removing the corpus luteum
blocks.prompt: In a woman who is not pregnant, the corpus luteum is removed on day 21. Predict the effects on progesterone, the endometrium and the pituitary.

steps.text: Progesterone (and oestradiol and inhibin A) fall abruptly because the corpus luteum was their source.
Loss of progesterone causes spiral artery constriction, ischaemia and shedding of the functional layer: menstruation starts early.
Removal of negative feedback lets FSH rise, starting recruitment of the next cohort of follicles.

blocks.answer: Progesterone falls, menstruation starts early and FSH rises as feedback is released.

items: Follicular phase: FSH recruits follicles; oestradiol rises; proliferative endometrium.
Ovulation: sustained high oestradiol causes positive feedback and an LH surge; ovulation about 36 hours after surge onset.
Luteal phase: corpus luteum secretes progesterone; secretory endometrium; progesterone raises body temperature.
Menstruation follows the fall in progesterone and oestradiol when the corpus luteum regresses.
Luteal phase is about 14 days; cycle-length variation arises in the follicular phase.

blocks.title: The switch from negative to positive feedback
blocks.text: Oestradiol is a negative feedback signal at low and moderate levels, but a high concentration sustained for about 2 days acts positively on the hypothalamic-pituitary unit and creates the LH surge. This is one of the few positive feedback loops in endocrinology, and it is terminated by ovulation and luteinisation, after which progesterone returns the system to negative feedback.

blocks.title: Do not call the whole cycle the 'follicular phase'
blocks.text: The ovarian cycle (follicular, ovulation, luteal) and the endometrial cycle (menstrual, proliferative, secretory) use different names for overlapping periods. The proliferative phase corresponds to the late follicular phase and the secretory phase corresponds to the luteal phase.

points: The cycle starts on day 1 of menstruation; follicular phase length varies while the luteal phase is about 14 days.
FSH recruits follicles; thecal LH-driven androgens are aromatised by FSH-stimulated granulosa cells to oestradiol, which proliferates the endometrium.
Sustained high oestradiol causes positive feedback and an LH surge, triggering ovulation about 36 hours later and formation of the corpus luteum.
Progesterone from the corpus luteum produces the secretory endometrium; its fall with luteolysis causes spiral artery constriction and menstruation.

questions.stem: Which hormone dominates the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle?

options.text: Progesterone from the corpus luteum
FSH from the anterior pituitary
Inhibin B from granulosa cells
Human chorionic gonadotrophin

distractorRationale.b: FSH is suppressed during the luteal phase.
distractorRationale.c: Inhibin B is mainly follicular; inhibin A rises in the luteal phase.
distractorRationale.d: hCG is made by the embryo after implantation and is absent in a non-pregnant cycle.

questions.explanation: After ovulation, the corpus luteum secretes large amounts of progesterone with some oestradiol. Progesterone converts the endometrium to a secretory state and inhibits gonadotrophin secretion.

questions.stem: In the two-cell, two-gonadotrophin model of oestradiol synthesis, which description is correct?

options.text: LH stimulates theca cells to make androgens, which FSH-stimulated granulosa cells aromatise to oestradiol
FSH stimulates theca cells to make oestradiol directly
LH stimulates granulosa cells to aromatise androgens, while FSH stimulates theca cells to make androgens
Oestradiol is made only by the corpus luteum

questions.correctOptionText: LH stimulates theca cells to make androgens, which FSH-stimulated granulosa cells aromatise to oestradiol

distractorRationale.b: Theca cells make androgens, not oestradiol directly.
distractorRationale.c: The roles of LH and FSH are reversed.
distractorRationale.d: Follicles are the main source of oestradiol in the follicular phase.

questions.explanation: Theca cells respond to LH and supply androgens; granulosa cells respond to FSH, express aromatase and convert androgens to oestradiol. Both gonadotrophins are therefore needed.

questions.stem: Which event triggers the mid-cycle LH surge?

options.text: Sustained high oestradiol from the dominant follicle exerting positive feedback
A fall in oestradiol removing negative feedback
A rise in progesterone from the corpus luteum
A fall in inhibin B alone

questions.correctOptionText: Sustained high oestradiol from the dominant follicle exerting positive feedback

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the high oestradiol threshold is the signal that the follicle is mature.
distractorRationale.b: Falling oestradiol would not cause an LH surge.
distractorRationale.c: Progesterone rises after the surge from the corpus luteum.
distractorRationale.d: Inhibin acts on FSH and does not cause the LH surge.

questions.explanation: Oestradiol is usually inhibitory, but when it is high for about two days the hypothalamic-pituitary unit responds with increased GnRH pulses and gonadotroph sensitivity, giving a surge of LH that triggers ovulation.

questions.stem: A biopsy of the endometrium shows tortuous glands containing glycogen-rich secretions, oedematous stroma and coiled spiral arteries. Which hormonal state does this indicate?

options.text: Progesterone dominance (luteal phase)
Unopposed oestradiol (early follicular phase)
Falling progesterone and oestradiol after luteolysis
High FSH and low progesterone before menstruation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is the secretory endometrium.
distractorRationale.b: Oestradiol alone gives proliferative endometrium with straight glands.
distractorRationale.c: Falling hormones produce ischaemia and shedding.
distractorRationale.d: This pattern does not describe a secretory endometrium.

questions.explanation: Progesterone, acting on an oestrogen-primed endometrium, makes glands tortuous and secretory, stroma oedematous and spiral arteries coiled, preparing the lining for implantation.

questions.stem: What is the immediate cause of menstruation in a non-pregnant cycle?

options.text: Fall in progesterone and oestradiol after corpus luteum regression, causing spiral artery constriction and ischaemia
The LH surge, which breaks down the endometrium
A rise in progesterone that dissolves the functional layer
Direct action of FSH on endometrial glands

questions.correctOptionText: Fall in progesterone and oestradiol after corpus luteum regression, causing spiral artery constriction and ischaemia

distractorRationale.a: Correct: withdrawal of hormonal support leads to shedding.
distractorRationale.b: The LH surge occurs about two weeks earlier and triggers ovulation.
distractorRationale.d: FSH acts on the ovary, not the endometrium.

questions.explanation: If implantation does not occur, the corpus luteum regresses and hormone support is withdrawn. Spiral arteries constrict, the functional layer becomes ischaemic and is shed, while the basal layer regenerates the lining.

questions.stem: Variation in menstrual cycle length between women arises mainly from differences in the length of the luteal phase.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The luteal phase is relatively constant at about 14 days, set by the lifespan of the corpus luteum. Differences in cycle length arise mainly from the variable length of the follicular phase.

questions.stem: A woman has regular 32-day cycles. Assuming the luteal phase is 14 days, on which day of the cycle (day 1 = first day of menstruation) is ovulation expected?
questions.explanation: Ovulation occurs about 14 days before the next menstruation, so the day is 32 - 14 = 18. Her follicular phase is therefore longer than the textbook 14 days.

questions.stem: A woman has regular 35-day cycles with a 14-day luteal phase. Sperm can survive up to 5 days in the female tract. Counting day 1 as the first day of menstruation, what is the first day of the fertile window, defined as 5 days before ovulation?
questions.explanation: Ovulation is on day 35 - 14 = 21. The fertile window opens 5 days earlier, on day 21 - 5 = 16, because sperm can survive for up to 5 days and the oocyte survives only about a day after ovulation.

questions.stem: Describe the follicular, ovulatory and luteal phases of the ovarian cycle, naming the dominant hormones in each and the corresponding changes in the endometrium.
markingGuide: Follicular phase: FSH recruits follicles, a dominant follicle emerges, oestradiol rises (theca androgens aromatised by granulosa cells)
Oestradiol causes proliferative endometrium: proliferation of glands, stroma and spiral arteries
Ovulation: LH surge causes release of the oocyte about 36 hours after surge onset
Luteal phase: corpus luteum secretes progesterone (with oestradiol and inhibin A), lasting about 14 days
Progesterone causes secretory endometrium: tortuous glycogen-secreting glands, oedematous stroma, coiled spiral arteries
Fall in hormones after luteolysis causes menstruation of the functional layer
questions.explanation: The ovarian hormones sequentially remodel the endometrium so that it is receptive for a few days in the luteal phase. If no pregnancy occurs, the withdrawal of progesterone ends the cycle.

questions.stem: Explain the positive feedback mechanism that produces the LH surge, contrasting it with the usual negative feedback of oestradiol, and say how the surge leads to ovulation and what ends it.
markingGuide: Early follicular: moderate oestradiol and inhibin B exert negative feedback on FSH and LH
As the dominant follicle matures, oestradiol rises to a high level sustained for about 2 days
High sustained oestradiol switches to positive feedback at the hypothalamus and pituitary, increasing GnRH pulses and gonadotroph sensitivity
A large LH surge (with a smaller FSH surge) results
LH surge completes meiosis I of the oocyte, causes follicle wall breakdown and ovulation about 36 hours after onset, and luteinisation to form the corpus luteum
The surge ends after ovulation as follicular oestradiol falls and progesterone from the corpus luteum restores negative feedback
questions.explanation: The positive feedback loop signals follicular maturity and synchronises ovulation. It is self-limiting because the follicle that generated it is transformed into the corpus luteum.
